cells.why: Redis here: matched SET 91,600/s with p99 4.9 ms, default 144,000 to 155,000/s (memtier). E-02's pipeline ceilings sit 5 to 60 times above the matched rows and only 3 to 5 times above the default rows, so no build is stopped, but no kernel ran through the RESP gateway at speed. The held-row clause holds: 81 ns in process against a 1.26 ms GET.
cells.closes: memtier through the RESP gateway on a real kernel, same hold as Redis: about 92,000 persisted SETs/s at 200 connections with p99 under 4.9 ms. The default pipeline-16 rows need a memory rung or the native step.
cells.why2: Redis's matched row here is about 92,000 SETs a second at p99 4.9 ms with memtier. E-02's bare pipeline ceiling is 5 to 60 times above the matched rows, but no fero kernel has run through memtier. The in-process read clause holds (81 ns through data, E-44); a row with no `memory` rung meets Redis's default rows with `persisted`, a thin margin but not a measured loss.

cells.why: Q `mix` has a `memory` rung for JetStream's default row (p99 0.55 ms). At the pipeline floor that rung reads 0.57 ms in TS, a tie, and 0.33 ms in Rust, at 50,000 writes/s and never with one write in flight, so the native step carries that row. Matched, group commit beats JetStream's 3,668 msgs/s by design, but its 1.31 ms single-publisher p99 beats every real-disk tail E-02 measured.
cells.closes: `nats bench js` through the JetStream gateway on a real kernel with one write in flight: `persisted` against sync always, and the `memory` rung against JetStream's default. The TS phase first; the native step if TS only ties.
cells.why2: The `memory` rung is the matching rung for JetStream's default. E-02's bare pipeline reads p99 0.57 ms in TS, a tie with JetStream's 0.55 ms, and 0.33 ms in Rust, a win, both at 50,000 a second and not with one write in flight. So the native phase carries the default row; the matched one-publisher row (JetStream p99 1.31 ms) is open in both phases.

cells.why: This row's only durable rung is `persisted`. JetStream's default acks one publisher at p99 0.55 ms, below C = 0.73 ms, the floor of any persisted commit on this box, so the row cannot win JetStream's default single-publisher row (both measured). PERF-01 makes that win a MUST while the user's list of accepted losses is empty; the matched rows stay open.

JetStream's default acks one publisher at p99 0.55 ms, below that floor, so the default row cannot be won, and PERF-01 allows no loss today. The matched rows stay open (JetStream 1,228 acks a second, p99 1.31 ms).

But that pipeline has no Raft and no fold, and E-11's simple host around the real TS Raft port read 10 to 11 ms at 10,000 writes/s.
cells.closes: The phase-2 pin: p99 commit at 50,000 writes/s on a pipelined kernel with the real Raft core, with the `fio` floor beside it. The native bar (C + 0.5 ms) is judged at the native step.
cells.why2: TS bar 5.7 ms: E-02's bare pipeline reads p99 4.3 ms (3.7 ms with the kernel on a worker), but E-11's real TS Raft on a simple host read 10 ms. Native bar 1.23 ms: the Rust pipeline reads 1.58 ms on this one shared disk and 0.67 ms with emulated separate disks; etcd itself reads 1.73 ms here. A `ts→rs` row is judged on the TS bar first and the native bar after its step; both are open.

cells.why: Judge 2 was right. E-02's TS pipeline commits 2.8 M appends a second (1.53 M with a client front, E-39), 30 to 56 times the TS bars, but it is a ceiling with no Raft core, no L2 and no fold, which is why both judges left PERF-08 open on the same pipeline. The one run on the real TS Raft port was at 10,000 writes a second and took 0.6 to 0.7 of a core per process with one group (E-11), and the native bars this row owes at its native step are open too (Rust tops out at 2.2 to 4.1 M on this disk against 2 M per writer).
cells.closes: Pins on the real kernel: phase 2 for the TS bars (50,000 a second per process and per writer through the real Raft core, L2 and the fold), the native build for the native bars.

Where a row has `ridx`, ReadIndex gives the one round trip with no fsync by construction.

cells.why2: A held-row read through data took 81 ns (E-44), and where the row holds W `ridx` or `lease` a `fresh` read is one round and no fsync by construction. But the conditional op at the writer (3 µs) and the method call whose caller is the writer (10 µs) were not timed on any v5 kernel.

Where a row has `ridx`, ReadIndex gives the one round trip with no fsync by construction.

cells.why: As the other rows, with one weak point: a call that waits on the daemon costs about 33 µs over a socket (E-03), against 3 and 10 µs. The row avoids it only if the app's process judges ops itself for the groups its host leads and feeds the daemon through the shared-memory ring (15 ns a record). That path was not built.

cells.why2: A request and its reply to the daemon over a socket cost 33 µs (E-03), 10 times the 3 µs bar. With the shared-memory ring (A-30) records cross at 15 ns in batches, but one op at a time was not timed, so this is a weak point, not a measured ceiling.

cells.why: Step 1: BUY's writer is the outside server, which cannot run fero's conditions or ops. Step 2: so a conditional op is a client read plus a publish, each a round trip, retried on conflict: about 4 ms an op, with 34 % of publishes wasted at 8 writers (E-44). Step 3: one loopback round trip alone is 31 to 58 µs (E-01), over the 3 µs bar, and no method call can have the writer as its caller.
cells.why2: The judge is the client: a conditional write on JetStream is a read and a publish, each a round trip, about 4 ms an op, with 34 % of publishes wasted under 8 writers (E-44). The bar is 3 µs at the writer.

cells.why: With quiet groups (A-12), 2,000 idle groups sent nothing and cost 0.15 % of a core on the TS Raft port, 0.10 % on etcd's raft in Go and 0.04 % on raft-rs. A member with 99 links pinged every 500 ms plus 2,000 quiet groups used 0.95 % of a core in Node (0.94 to 0.99) and 0.33 % in Rust, and n = 100 makes 19,800 frames/s. It holds, narrowly in TS and only up to n = 100.
cells.why2: With quiet groups (A-12), 2,000 idle groups cost 0.15 % of a core on the real TS Raft port, 0.10 % in Go and 0.04 % in Rust, and sent no frames of their own (E-11). At n = 100 pairwise pings make 19,800 frames a second, and a Node member with 99 links and 2,000 quiet groups used 0.95 % of a core, 0.33 % in Rust (E-25). The TS margin at n = 100 is thin.

cells.why: E-25's count, on Kafka's cited defaults: idle follower fetches are pairwise each way every 500 ms, so above about 10,000 partitions ISR sends 34,456 to 39,700 frames/s at n = 100, over the bar of about 20,000. It is a count, not a run, and the fetch wait is a constant: a weak point, not a failure by design.
cells.closes: A run of ISR's idle fetch sessions at n = 100 with the fetch wait sized to `ping.ms`.
cells.why2: Kafka-style idle fetches are pairwise each way: about 34,000 to 40,000 frames a second at n = 100 from about 1e4 partitions, by E-25's count with Kafka's 500 ms wait, over the cap of about 20,000. A longer wait is a constant, so this is a weak point, not a failure by design.

cells.why: The frames clause holds by E-25's count: one session per server to the controller, 400 frames/s at n = 100. The CPU clause was not measured: what 2,000 idle loglets cost one process is unknown.
cells.closes: A run of 2,000 idle loglets in one process.
cells.why2: Sessions to a controller make 400 frames a second at n = 100 by E-25's count, far under the cap. The CPU of 2,000 idle loglets in one process was not measured.

cells.why: OBJ sends no frames, but each group's lease is renewed by a conditional PUT: 500 to 50,000 PUTs/s at 1,000 to 100,000 resources (E-25's count). So an idle group does send something of its own unless leases go quiet, and the row does not yet say they do.
cells.closes: A design for quiet leases, then a run of 2,000 idle groups in one process.
cells.why2: It sends no idle frames, but a lease renewed every 2 s per group is a PUT each time: 1,000 PUTs a second for 2,000 idle groups, unless leases go quiet (E-25, a count). So idle groups do send something of their own as the row stands.

cells.why: v4's idle traffic at n = 100 is about 20,000 frames/s (DESIGN-V5 section 8), at the bar. What 2,000 idle resources cost one process was not measured; each v4 resource is its own cluster with its own heartbeats.
cells.closes: A v4 run with 2,000 idle resources in one process; none is planned.
cells.why2: v4 sends about 20,000 idle frames a second at n = 100 (DESIGN-V5 section 8), at the cap. The cost of 2,000 idle resources in one process was not measured.

cells.why: With quiet groups (A-12), 2,000 idle groups sent nothing and cost 0.15 % of a core on the TS Raft port, 0.10 % on etcd's raft in Go and 0.04 % on raft-rs. A member with 99 links pinged every 500 ms plus 2,000 quiet groups used 0.95 % of a core in Node (0.94 to 0.99) and 0.33 % in Rust, and n = 100 makes 19,800 frames/s. It holds, narrowly in TS and only up to n = 100.
cells.why2: With quiet groups (A-12), 2,000 idle groups cost 0.15 % of a core on the real TS Raft port, 0.10 % in Go and 0.04 % in Rust, and sent no frames of their own (E-11). At n = 100 pairwise pings make 19,800 frames a second, and a Node member with 99 links and 2,000 quiet groups used 0.95 % of a core, 0.33 % in Rust (E-25). The TS margin at n = 100 is thin.

cells.why: Judge 2 was right, though the monitor it calls unbuilt did run in E-22's prototype: every caught-up replica's rows equalled a fresh fold of the log on every seed. That was one thread, and rows by value only. The design is right: a log entry is data's change record under a header that wraps it (about 3.9 B a record, E-19), and E-22's prototype folds records verbatim. But the v5 header and codec are phase-1 work, and two things are owed: byte values, which API.md refuses and every protocol carries (E-45), and whether a view stream carries data's `move` records (E-22). No v5 codec has a round-trip test.
cells.closes: Phase 1: the record header and the value encoding fixed, with codec round-trip tests in both repos.
cells.why2: The designs carry data's records as log entries and wrap them in headers (a per-slot sequence adds 3.9 B a record, E-19). But the v5 record format is not fixed: values must allow bytes (E-45) and a format V8 decodes whole is planned (A-13). No round-trip test exists for it.

cells.why2: V4-47's tests are in today's battery: what user code throws at a commit goes to the composer's Fault in api/substrate.ts (CLAUDE.md, the two seams).

cells.why: Judge 2 was right. A mutation probe run here on E-22's prototype broke the rule: after a field-level write, a row read through a `filter` view was not frozen, and writing to it changed what that server held (999 against 5 on the others), which the prototype's own fold monitor then reported. The seam freezes rows on `get` and `snapshot`, not rows read through data's views, so a frozen row on every hand-out path, and its cost against the 100 ns read, is not shown.
